nameStory: The name 'blewit' comes from the old English word 'blue hat,' referring to this mushroom's distinctive bluish-purple coloring that's especially vibrant when young. Some folks also call it the 'wood blewit' since it's commonly found among fallen logs and leaf litter in woodlands, helping distinguish it from its field-dwelling cousin.
description: The blewit is a medium to large mushroom with a striking blue-purple color that fades to brownish tones with age. Its smooth, rounded cap can reach 3-6 inches across, sitting atop a sturdy stem that often shows the same purple hues. The gills underneath are crowded together and share that characteristic blue-violet coloring when fresh. This eye-catching fungus is hard to miss once you know what to look for!

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Starts bright blue-purple when young, fading to brownish-lilac with age. Feels smooth and slightly sticky when moist, with edges that curl inward on young specimens.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Crowded, attached to the stem, starting pale blue-violet and becoming pinkish-buff as spores develop. Run your finger along them - they feel soft and closely packed.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Solid and fibrous with a swollen base, often showing purple streaks or overall blue-violet coloring, especially near the top. Feels firm but can be somewhat stringy.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Pleasant, sweet, and fruity - often described as perfume-like or floral. The aroma becomes more pronounced when you crush a piece of the flesh.

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Pale pink to pinkish-buff colored. Place the cap gill-side down on white paper overnight to see this diagnostic feature clearly.

habitat: Look for blewits in both deciduous and coniferous woodlands throughout New England, often growing in leaf litter, compost piles, or near decaying wood. They particularly love rich, organic soil in mixed forests with oak, maple, and pine. You might also spot them in wood chip mulch around gardens or parks.

seasonality.spring: Rarely found in spring, though occasional specimens may appear during warm, wet periods in late spring after the ground has thoroughly thawed.
seasonality.summer: Uncommon during summer months, but may fruit during cool, rainy periods when temperatures drop and moisture levels stay high.
seasonality.fall: Peak season! Look for fresh blewits from September through November, especially after autumn rains when they emerge in impressive clusters.
seasonality.winter: Can occasionally fruit during mild winter spells or under snow cover, but most specimens will be old and deteriorated by this time.

funFact: Blewits are one of the few mushrooms that actually improve in flavor after being frozen - commercial growers discovered that freezing breaks down tough cell walls and concentrates the sweet, nutty taste that has made them popular in European cuisine for centuries!
confusionNotes: Most dangerous look-alikes lack the blewit's distinctive sweet, perfumed smell and pinkish spore print. Young specimens might be confused with some purple Cortinarius species, but those have rusty-brown spore prints and often grow directly from soil rather than leaf litter. Remember the phrase: 'Pink print, sweet scent, blewit sent!'
contextualKnowledge: This mushroom has gone through several scientific name changes over the decades - you might see it listed as Lepista nuda or Clitocybe nuda in older field guides. The recent reassignment to Collybia in 2023 reflects new DNA research, but don't worry - it's still the same purple beauty regardless of what scientists decide to call it!
compareHints: Unlike other Collybia species in New England which tend to be brown or white, the blewit stands out with its blue-purple coloration and sweet fragrance. The related Flowery Blewit (Collybia irina) is much paler and lacks the strong blue tones, while species like the Lentil Shanklet are tiny parasitic mushrooms that grow on other fungi rather than in leaf litter.
